hero.title: Visualizing Adaptive and Transformative Governance
hero.subtitle: Qatar at the nexus of local, regional, transnational and global change
hero.standfirst: A two year research programme at the College of Public Policy, Hamad Bin Khalifa University, examining how governance systems in Qatar adapt under uncertainty and when adaptation becomes structural change. Five case studies, four colleges, five external partners.
hero.metadata: Hamad Bin Khalifa University Signature Research Grant · July 2025 to July 2027 · Project Lead Dr. Evren Tok

studies.heading: Adaptive governance, and when it becomes transformative
body: Adaptive governance is the iterative fine tuning of policy under uncertainty, driven by data and by feedback from implementation. Transformative governance is different in kind: a durable shift in authority, resources or rules. The two are connected. Repeated adaptation can trigger a transformative leap, and a transformative leap often unlocks adaptation that was previously blocked.

This project treats the boundary between them as an empirical question rather than a theoretical one. Each case is coded for adaptive signals, meaning real time feedback loops and revision frequency, and for transformative markers, meaning new mandates, budget reallocations and new institutions. The point is to locate where incremental learning tips into systemic change.

Qatar is a productive place to ask this. It sits at a nexus of local, national, regional and transnational pressure, and its institutions have absorbed technological disruption, climate stress and shifting geopolitical alignment inside a compressed period. The country does not only adapt to these pressures. It also shapes governance discourse across scales, which makes it a case that speaks to global debates rather than a case that only illustrates them.

definitions.text: Real time feedback loops. Revision frequency. Evidence that a policy instrument is being tuned rather than merely administered.
New mandates. Budget reallocation. New institutions. Evidence that authority or rules have moved, not just settings.
The institutional room in which experimentation is permitted, recorded and fed back into decisions.

cases.heading: Five cases, one comparison
cases.intro: Each case was selected against four criteria: state sponsorship, relevance across more than one scale, accessible data, and alignment with Qatar National Vision 2030. Each is studied through document analysis, structured interviews and participatory methods. A synthesis matrix then compares them, and that comparison is what produces the framework.

items.label: Case one
items.title: Digital policy labs
items.description: How regulatory experimentation is organised inside Qatar's digital transformation agenda, and what happens to a rule once a lab has tested it.
items.leads: Led by Dr. Georgios Dimitropoulos and Dr. Kehinde Olaoye, College of Law, with practitioner input from the Ministry of Communication and Information Technology and Ibtechar.

items.label: Case two
items.title: Smart city platforms
items.description: Urban services as a governance layer: what municipal data changes about who decides, how fast, and on whose evidence.
items.leads: Led by Dr. Esmat Zaidan, College of Public Policy, with Dr. Sukaina Nasrawi at ESCWA.

items.label: Case three
items.title: Strategic foresight and national narratives
items.description: How foresight units inside government translate long horizon scenarios into present decisions, and how national narratives constrain what can be planned for.
items.leads: Led by Dr. Evren Tok, College of Public Policy.

items.label: Case four
items.title: Crowdsourced sentiment
items.description: Arabic social media data from the FIFA World Cup 2022, analysed to show how daily sentiment reporting fed transport, security and crowd decisions in real time.
items.leads: Led by Dr. George Mikros, College of Humanities and Social Sciences.

items.label: Case five
items.title: Humanitarian diplomacy
items.description: Qatar's humanitarian and diplomatic practice as a form of governance that operates across borders, read through the concept of nested power.
items.leads: Led by Dr. Abdulfatah Mohamed, College of Islamic Studies, with H.E. Dr. Abdulaziz Al Horr at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

items.heading: Objective one. Examine adaptive governance in practice.
items.body: Map actor constellations, institutional dynamics and policy innovations across the five cases, then compare them in a synthesis matrix to identify where adaptive and transformative practice actually emerges and whether it can be scaled.

items.heading: Objective two. Build tools that make adaptive capacity visible.
items.body: Foresight scenarios, computational linguistic dashboards and an interactive governance dashboard built in Tableau, showing the linkages, feedback loops and actor networks that make up the governance ecosystem. Co designed with ministries and municipalities so that they are usable rather than illustrative.

items.heading: Objective three. Build capacity.
items.body: A training course and certificate, two new co taught graduate courses, integration into existing programmes at the College of Public Policy, the College of Law and the College of Humanities and Social Sciences, and supervised student research.

items.heading: Objective four. Advance theory and inform reform.
items.body: Peer reviewed case articles, a systematic review, a comparative policy paper and a framework article, benchmarked against global governance debates rather than written only for a local audience.

corpus.heading: The evidence base
body: The project opened with a systematic review of the adaptive governance literature. The search returned 1,172 records. Screening reduced these to 272 that met the inclusion criteria, and full text assessment narrowed that further against a strict definition of adaptive governance as a core concept rather than a passing reference.

The corpus is published here in full. Each record carries its title, authors, year, outlet, a link to the source, and the reason it was kept or excluded. You can filter by country, region, year, theme and method, and search across the set.

It is also what drives the globe on this page. Each country is raised and lit in proportion to the number of studies the corpus holds from it. The distribution is uneven, and that unevenness is a finding: adaptive governance scholarship clusters in a small number of settings, and the Gulf is thin. Part of what this project is doing is making that thinner region legible.

roadmap.heading: Roadmap
roadmap.intro: Twenty four months, five work packages, running in parallel with a synthesis phase at the end. Status is updated as phases close.

phases.title: Foundational research. September 2025 to December 2025.
phases.body: Systematic search, screening, analysis, review article drafted. Complete.

phases.title: Work package one. Digital transformation. November 2025 to October 2026.
phases.body: Document review and interviews, then analysis, then the article on policy labs. Analysis complete, article in drafting.

phases.title: Work package two. Cities and public services. December 2025 to July 2027.
phases.body: Municipal data and interviews, then analysis from October 2026, then the article on smart city platforms.

phases.title: Work package three. Data, narratives and foresight. November 2025 to July 2027.
phases.body: Documents, datasets and interviews, then analysis from October 2026, then the article on foresight.

phases.title: Work package four. Computational linguistics. November 2025 to May 2027.
phases.body: Corpus construction and model setup, then text mining and validation from October 2026, then the article on crowdsourced sentiment.

phases.title: Work package five. Agile humanitarian governance. November 2025 to May 2027.
phases.body: Reports and interviews, then analysis from October 2026, then the article on humanitarian governance.

phases.title: Interactive governance dashboard. October 2025 to August 2027.
phases.body: Built in Tableau across the life of the project, refreshed as each work package reports.

phases.title: Synthesis and dissemination. April 2027 to September 2027.
phases.body: Consolidated findings, comparative synthesis policy paper, framework article.

phases.title: Capacity building. September 2026 to June 2027.
phases.body: Curriculum design, then delivery of the training course and certificate.

roadmap.note: Dates reflect the approved research plan. Where a phase has moved, the status line records it.

outputs.heading: Outputs
outputs.intro: Published work, tools and teaching material. Items appear here when they are public.

items.title: Peer reviewed articles
items.body: One article per case, plus a systematic review of adaptive governance frameworks.

items.title: Comparative synthesis policy paper
items.body: Lessons from the five cases set against experience elsewhere, written for policy readers rather than for the literature.

items.title: Adaptive governance framework article
items.body: A working model for agencies, connected to Qatar National Vision 2030 and to regional agendas.

items.title: Interactive governance dashboard
items.body: A visualization of governance linkages, feedback loops and actor networks across the cases.

items.title: Training course and certificate
items.body: Practical work on decision making under uncertainty and on operating inside adaptive policy spaces, for professionals and students.

items.title: Graduate courses
items.body: Adaptive and Transformative Governance in the Arab World. Data Driven Governance and Policy Innovation. Both co taught.

collaborate.heading: Get in touch
collaborate.intro: We are interested in three kinds of contact.

audiences.label: Researchers.
audiences.text: If you work on adaptive or transformative governance, on foresight in government, or on any of the five cases, we are open to joint papers, panels and comparative extensions of the framework to other Gulf states.

audiences.label: Government and institutional partners.
audiences.text: If you are running something that looks like an adaptive space, a policy lab, a foresight unit, a data driven service, we would like to hear about it, and where appropriate to study it.

audiences.label: Students.
audiences.text: Capstone and dissertation topics that extend the framework or use project data are supervised through the College of Public Policy.
